name: application-service
intent: Give each externally callable business use case a thin, stateless application boundary that translates a request, loads the required aggregates, delegates every invariant to the domain model, commits one local unit of work, and returns a stable result without exposing domain objects.
problem: A business operation may need to load several aggregates, ask a domain service for a decision, persist the result, record an event and commit atomically. If an HTTP controller, CLI command, queue handler and scheduler each assemble that sequence, transaction scope, authorization, idempotency, error mapping and event handling drift. The application service gives that use case one explicit owner, while the domain model remains the owner of business truth.
context: A deliberately rich domain model (Entity, Aggregate, Value Object, Domain Service and Repository) with one or more use cases that cross object or repository boundaries, multiple inbound clients, and a local transaction boundary that must be consistent for all of them. The model stays persistence-ignorant, so the application layer supplies the unit of work and the boundary concerns the model should not carry: authorization, tenant and user resolution, idempotency, input and DTO translation, audit, and durable domain-event dispatch.
benefits: Every use case has exactly one owner: callers delegate instead of re-assembling steps, so ordering, authorization, error handling and transaction scope cannot diverge between the web API, the CLI and the queue consumer.
Domain objects stay framework- and persistence-ignorant: orchestration, mapping and infrastructure calls live one layer out, which is what makes the model independently testable and reusable.
The transaction boundary becomes a property of the use case rather than of an adapter: one method is one unit of work, so atomicity is declared once and checked in one place.
Application-level concerns (input validation, permission checks, idempotency keys, event publication, audit) attach at the boundary once, instead of in every client and every entity.
Callers receive DTOs or result objects, so the model can change without breaking presentation contracts and presentation can change without touching the model.
Collaborators are ports (repositories, domain services, gateways, clock, id generator), so the orchestration can be unit-tested with fakes and no database or web server.
Idempotency keys and deduplication tables can be committed atomically with the business state change, making 'execute exactly once' a property of the use case rather than the transport layer.
Domain events can be stored in the same transaction as the state change (outbox pattern), eliminating the dual-write problem where the DB commits but the event publish fails.
tradeoffs: An extra layer plus DTO translation: a use case that loads one aggregate by id becomes a pass-through method that adds files, mapping code and indirection without adding information.
The thin-orchestrator rule is unenforced by the language: once a service method branches on business state, the decision has leaked out of the model and nothing fails until the model is anemic.
Per-noun services drift into god classes whose constructor is the union of every use case's dependencies; the class then grows one method per verb and becomes the hardest file to change.

Owning the transaction couples orchestration to the persistence mechanism and makes composing two services into one larger unit of work harder; self-invoked or nested transactional methods produce half-committed surprises.

Framework-absorbed variants hide transaction and error handling behind proxies and interceptors (Spring AOP, ABP unit of work, NestJS interceptors), so failures look like 'the write was committed anyway' and are hard to see in the code.
Long use cases keep a database transaction open across remote calls, holding locks for the duration of network I/O and hurting throughput.
Read paths must either load aggregates through the write-side model or add a separate read model/DTO projection; the naive version pays aggregate-loading cost for every query.
MediatR-style blanket pipeline behaviors (transaction wrapping every handler) hold locks across queries that never needed a transaction, inflating latency for read-heavy workloads.

participants.responsibility: Owns one use case (or a cohesive set of operations on one aggregate): stateless, takes a request DTO, loads what it needs, delegates decisions to the model, persists, publishes, returns a response DTO, and owns the transaction boundary.

Controller, CLI command, queue consumer or scheduled job: translates transport input into a request, calls the service, translates the result into a response; contains no business logic and no transaction management of its own.
Entity, Aggregate, Value Object and Domain Service decide and enforce the business rules; they are unaware of the service, the DTOs, the transaction and the callers.
Load and persist aggregates for the use case; the service coordinates them, and the unit of work (not the repository) decides when the whole use case commits or rolls back.
Define the input and output of the use case in its own terms, so neither transport types nor domain objects cross the boundary.

A table or distributed cache that records which commands have been processed, committed in the same transaction as the business state change so that retrying a message cannot double-apply the use case.

Publishes the events the model raised as part of the use case, preferably after the state change is durable (after-commit, outbox, or transactional outbox table) so publication and persistence cannot disagree.

use_cases: A web API, a CLI command and a queue consumer must execute the same 'place an order' operation: all three call one service method, so validation, authorization, transaction and event publication cannot drift.

A use case spanning several aggregates: a domain service decides whether a transfer is permitted, the application service loads both accounts, invokes the decision, saves the outcome and publishes the event inside one transaction (Vernon's transactional application service).

CQRS systems: commands are executed by application services or command handlers, while queries bypass the domain model through a dedicated read model. The application service loads the aggregate, calls its behaviour, persists, and publishes domain events - all inside one transaction.
Background and batch processing where the same use case must run without an HTTP request, with its own transaction, logging and retry policy.
Greenfield domain modelling where per-aggregate CRUD services are the first cut and are then refined into one operation per use case as dependencies and rules grow.
Multi-tenant or heavily audited applications where the boundary is the single place to resolve the current user/tenant, check permission and record the audit entry for a business operation.

Saga / process manager orchestration: an application service drives a multi-step workflow across bounded contexts, loading a process-manager aggregate, advancing its state, persisting it, and dispatching commands to participant services; each step is its own transaction with compensating transactions for failure.

Event-driven workflows where a domain event triggers a use case that must atomically update business state and schedule or publish follow-on events (outbox pattern) so that downstream consumers receive every event exactly once.

Cross-bounded context integration: one bounded context's application service subscribes to published events from another, translates them into commands or queries, and coordinates the local response with its own transaction.

Vaughn Vernon's SaaSOvation identity/access and project-management examples: a ProductBacklogItem application service loads a Product aggregate, invokes its behavior and persists the new item under one transaction.

An NServiceBus endpoint handles a PlaceOrder command through a message handler: the handler coordinates the local repositories and outbox, while the endpoint's unit of work and recoverability policy make retries safe only when the use case is idempotent.

A FastAPI router injects a request-scoped application service and repository with Depends; the endpoint translates HTTP input, the service executes the domain command, and the response mapper returns a DTO rather than an aggregate.
avoid_when: The operation is a pass-through CRUD call on one aggregate: a repository or aggregate method is simpler, and an application service would add ceremony without owning a meaningful use case.
The logic is genuinely procedural and there is no rich domain model to protect: Transaction Script keeps one request's steps honest instead of creating empty entities plus an orchestration shell.

A framework already exposes a complete use-case boundary for a thin CRUD endpoint and no cross-object coordination is needed; adding another application-service layer only hides the real transaction owner.
The workload is read-dominated: use a query service, projection or CQRS read model rather than loading write-side aggregates to format a response.
The ORM session or DbContext already is the complete unit of work for a single operation; adding a service that only forwards get/save calls buys indirection, not a boundary.
The process spans multiple bounded contexts with independent databases: use a saga or process manager, because a local application-service transaction cannot commit across services.

The missing behavior is a domain decision that spans entities or aggregates but has no application sequencing concern: use a Domain Service for that stateless rule and let the application service only coordinate it.
You only need Fowler's generic Service Layer naming for a simple layered system and do not have DDD aggregates or invariants; do not imply that the DDD application-service constraints apply.
anti_patterns: Anemic domain model: business rules accumulate in the application service while entities become data bags, so the same rule must be re-implemented by every entry point; unlike a healthy application service, this replaces domain behavior instead of coordinating it.
God service: one class owns every verb for an aggregate and accumulates every dependency; unlike one-use-case services, it makes unrelated changes and transaction boundaries travel together.
Pass-through service: a method only calls repository.get(id) and repository.save(entity); unlike a meaningful application boundary, it adds ceremony without orchestration, policy or translation.

Domain logic in the service layer: an application method branches on balance or eligibility and mutates fields; unlike delegation to an aggregate or Domain Service, the invariant is not enforced by the model.
Entity leakage: controllers receive ORM entities or pass them back into services; unlike DTO boundaries, serialization, lazy loading and persistence state become part of the caller contract.
Transaction creep: the service opens a transaction before remote calls or lets repositories commit; unlike a short local unit of work, it holds locks across I/O and can leave partial outcomes.
Application-service chaining: one application service calls another to reuse orchestration; unlike composing one explicit use case, nested ownership obscures which boundary commits and rolls back.
Framework-absorbed transactions: every public method is annotated without a deliberate boundary; unlike an explicit use-case owner, proxy behavior and propagation hide when work commits.
Dual-write: the service commits business state and then publishes directly; unlike a transactional outbox, a crash between writes leaves consumers unaware of the committed change.
Idempotency forgotten: a queue consumer has no atomically stored command key; unlike an idempotent use case, retry delivery applies the operation twice.
N+1 repository calls: the service queries once per item in a loop; unlike a batch port, it holds the transaction open and magnifies latency and lock contention.
Infrastructure exceptions returned to callers: JPA, SQL or framework errors cross the boundary; unlike stable application errors, clients become coupled to persistence details.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: application logic (when, who, in what order), domain logic (what is true) and infrastructure (how it is stored or transported) live in different layers.
Single responsibility: one use case per method (or one class per use case), so there is exactly one reason to change.
Dependency inversion: services depend on repository and gateway interfaces owned by the application or domain, never on ORM, HTTP or framework types.
Tell, don't ask: ask the model to decide and act instead of reading its state and branching on it in the service.
Explicit transaction boundary: one unit of work per use case instead of per-statement autocommit.
Interface segregation at the boundary: clients depend on a narrow application interface, not on the model or the framework behind it.
Idempotency by design: record the command's idempotency key in the same transaction as the state change so retries are safe.
Events after commit: publish domain events only after the transaction commits successfully, using an outbox table or after-commit hook to prevent dual-write failures.
best_practices: Keep the service thin: load, delegate, persist, publish, return. If a method needs to branch on domain state, push that decision into the model.
One use case per method, and split by verb as soon as a per-noun service starts accumulating dependencies.
Inject ports through the constructor (or the framework's dependency injection) and never resolve collaborators from a global registry inside a method.
Accept request DTOs and return response DTOs or result objects; translate domain failures into a stable boundary error type instead of leaking ORM or framework exceptions.
Own the transaction explicitly and keep it short: commit once per use case, never hold it across remote calls, and publish events after the commit (outbox or after-commit hook).
Put application concerns here - authorization, idempotency, tenant/user resolution, input shape - and leave invariants to the entities, aggregates and domain services.
Give the service a boundary test (fakes for ports) plus a smaller number of integration tests that prove the transaction actually commits or rolls back.
Implement idempotency by committing an idempotency-key record in the same transaction as the business state change, then checking for that key at the start of the method before doing any work.

Classify errors at the boundary: domain rule violations become application-level exceptions (e.g. OrderNotPlaceable), infrastructure failures (DB, network) become separate error categories, never conflated with domain failures.
For query-only use cases, bypass the aggregate entirely and use a dedicated query service or read model; do not load aggregates just to extract a few fields for display.

When a use case must span services or bounded contexts, promote it to a saga or process manager rather than chaining application service calls — each participant's step is its own transaction with compensating logic for failures.
Keep method length bounded: a service method that grows past ~50 lines is a smell that domain logic has crept in and should be extracted to a domain service or policy.
Use a structured result type (Result<T>, Either<T, E> or equivalent) to represent both the happy path and domain-level failure without throwing exceptions for expected business outcomes.
Version the request and response DTOs independently from the domain model; the application service boundary is the stability contract with callers, not the domain classes.

related_patterns_notes.service-layer: The application service is the DDD-specific name for what Fowler's Service Layer establishes in a layered architecture. Application services are the thin, stateless variant of the Service Layer pattern, distinct from the richer 'operation script' variant which may carry application-level workflow logic.
related_patterns_notes.domain-service: Both live in the domain-model layer but serve different purposes: a domain service holds stateless domain logic that doesn't belong on a single entity or aggregate (e.g. a transfer-approval calculation spanning two accounts), while an application service orchestrates the use case (loading, sequencing, persisting). An application service may call a domain service, never the reverse.
related_patterns_notes.transaction-script: Both patterns organize business logic by use case. Transaction Script keeps the procedure as the unit of reuse and collocates all logic (domain and application) in one procedure. Application Service extracts a thin orchestrator and pushes domain logic into the model. When the domain is trivial or the crossover to rich domain behaviour has not yet happened, Transaction Script is the honest choice.
related_patterns_notes.domain-model: The application service protects the domain model from infrastructure and presentation concerns. It loads aggregates and calls their behaviour; it never implements domain rules itself. A healthy domain model is the proof that the application service is staying thin.
related_patterns_notes.repository: The application service depends on repository interfaces to load and persist aggregates. The repository should not commit — only the application-service-owned unit of work commits. This keeps the transaction boundary explicit and in one place.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: The application service opens the unit of work at the start of a use-case method and commits (or rolls back) at the end. This is the mechanism that makes one method equal one atomic transaction. The unit of work also tracks dirty and new aggregates so the service doesn't need to call save explicitly.
related_patterns_notes.domain-event: Domain objects raise events to record what happened; the application service (or a Domain Event Dispatcher participant) is responsible for publishing them. The outbox pattern is the recommended implementation: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business state change, then publish after commit. This eliminates the dual-write problem where the DB commits but event publication fails.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: DTOs are the only types that cross the application service boundary in either direction. Request DTOs carry caller intent into the service; response DTOs carry results back without exposing domain objects. This prevents entity leakage and decouples the model from presentation.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: When a business process spans multiple bounded contexts or services, a saga (or process manager) takes over orchestration from the application service. Each saga step runs in its own transaction with compensating transactions for failure. The application service that advances a saga step is itself a use case within the local bounded context.
related_patterns_notes.outbox: The transactional outbox pattern is the recommended implementation of the Domain Event Dispatcher participant. Instead of publishing events directly (which can fail after the DB commits), the application service writes events to an outbox table in the same transaction, and a separate relay process publishes them after commit.
related_patterns_notes.cqrs: CQRS separates read and write into different models. Application services (or command handlers) handle all writes: loading aggregates, enforcing invariants, persisting, publishing events. Queries go directly to a read model/projection without touching the domain model. The application service is the command side's orchestrator.
